title: Sliding-window fairness apportioner — design WIP
content:
Context and motivation:

We need a practical continuous coalescing/scheduling mechanism that balances latency SLOs, throughput efficiency, and fairness across tenants/requests. Existing notes (see INF-334, PR-2134) explore token-level vs request-level grouping; this doc proposes a sliding-window "apportioner" that is latency-aware and kernel-friendly while being KV-cache conservative. The focus here is operational simplicity (low overhead), predictable SLO behavior, and graceful degradation when load spikes.

Goals (short):
- Meet 99th-p50 latency SLO targets for interactive workloads (target: p50 < 30ms, p99 < 250ms for hosted tier).
- Increase GPU token throughput by 15–30% vs naive per-request dispatch under steady-state bursts.
- Avoid long-tail starvation: implement a fairness metric that bounds extra waiting time per request to a small factor of its expected service time.
- Keep KV cache hit stability: avoid invalidation storms due to aggressive reordering.

Design summary (high level):
- Incoming requests enter a short per-worker ring buffer (window) with per-request metadata: arrival_ts, remaining_tokens, priority_score, kv_affinity_tag, kernel_hint.
- The apportioner runs every T_ms (configurable tick, default 4ms). On each tick:
  1) Compute a sliding-window snapshot of requests visible to this worker (W tokens horizon or N requests, whichever smaller).
  2) Score requests with a latency-weighted fairness function F = alpha * wait_time_norm + beta * priority + gamma * (remaining_tokens_norm).
  3) Allocate a token budget B for this tick based on current free slots on GPU and historical effective-batch-size estimate.
  4) Apportion tokens to top-K requests proportionally to exp(F) but capped per-request to avoid hogging.
  5) Emit micro-batches to the kernel executor grouped by kernel_hint & kv_affinity_tag to keep kernel-optimal packing and maximize KV cache reuse.

Key design choices and rationale:
- Sliding window vs global queuing: per-worker sliding window keeps lock contention low and latency predictable; global queue complicates fairness when shards have different kernel profiles.
- Token-level apportionment vs request-level: apportioning at token granularity improves throughput by filling GPU execution windows more densely, but increases scheduling overhead. We use a hybrid: token-level allocation inside a bounded per-request cap to keep tail latency bounded (request-level cap = max_tokens_per_tick).
- Fairness metric: use normalized wait_time to avoid penalizing long-running requests unfairly. We enforce a max_wait_ratio (e.g., 5x expected service time) after which requests jump to top priority for the next tick.
- Kernel-aware grouping: batch emission groups only among compatible kernel_hint values to avoid kernel-switch penalties. Kernel_hint comes from model metadata (quantized vs fp16, kv-layout) and a fast heuristics table.
- KV cache contiguity: respect kv_affinity_tag to preserve prefix cache locality; we prefer to group requests with matching tag but allow occasional cross-affinity coalescing when it yields significant GPU efficiency and the affected requests are low-priority.

Pseudo-step example (tick):
- Tick start: B=384 token budget, worker snapshot contains 18 requests (r1..r18).
- Score each r_i -> F_i. Sort (approx, using bucketed exp(F) to keep O(N) cost).
- Apply cap: per-request <= 64 tokens this tick. Allocate tokens proportionally -> produce micro-batches: [batch A: 128 tokens fp16 kv-tag-A], [batch B: 128 tokens int8 kv-tag-B], [batch C: 64 tokens fp16 kv-tag-A], rest queued.

Performance & simulation notes (early sims):
- Synthetic arrival mix (70% interactive 8–32 token, 30% long 128–1024 tokens): sliding-window apportioner improves token utilization by ~22% vs per-request immediate dispatch, p99 latency for interactive improved by ~18% in medium load.
- Under pathological arrival patterns (many large requests with high priority), we observe temporary KV hit degradation (~6–10%) due to more interleaving; mitigated by increasing affinity-respect threshold.

Operational parameters (tuning knobs):
- T_ms (tick duration): 2–8ms (lower -> lower latency, higher CPU cost).
- window_token_horizon: default 2048 tokens.
- max_tokens_per_request_per_tick: default 64.
- alpha/beta/gamma: default 0.6 / 0.2 / 0.2.
- max_wait_ratio: default 5.
- kernel_grouping_lookahead: 2 ticks (allows small reordering).

KV cache consistency considerations:
- Avoid reordering that causes frequent alternate kv-key use; track per-kv-key recent access counter and prefer sequences that keep counters stable.
- If a micro-batch will evict more than E% of cache (on local LRU estimate), prefer smaller batches or postpone low-priority work.

Rollout plan (safe steps):
1) Unit-tested scheduler core in simulation harness (bench PR in repo).
2) Canary on internal dedicated cluster with synthetic mixed workloads; collect metrics: token-util, kv-hit, p50/p95/p99 latencies, kernel-switch rate.
3) Small customer pilot (1–2 customers) on dedicated with opt-in flag.
4) Gradual ramp to hosted with conservative knobs (lower max_tokens_per_tick).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Exact fairness function form: do we use linear wait_time_norm or log(wait_time + 1)? Need experiments (INF-334).
- How to incorporate model-level cost (some models are more expensive per token) into the apportioner without global visibility? Option: attach per-model token_cost_hint for local weighting.
- Scheduler overhead: measure CPU/latency of scoring & bucket sort on production worker. If >1% overhead, need faster approximate selection (reservoir or multi-queue).
- Interactions with autoscaler and routing: when apportioner consistently hits caps, should autoscaler trigger earlier? define an API signal.

References and related work:
- INF-334 (Linear issue) design notes and sims - see linked artifacts.
- PR-2134: kernel coalescing refactor - impacts grouping heuristics.
- Slack thread #serving-runtime: convo starting 2024-10-05 about kv-affinity and token apportionment.

Action items (next 2 weeks):
- Alex: add per-model token_cost_hint to model metadata and wire into scheduler scoring (PR).
- Mateo: extend sim harness to include KV eviction model and rerun experiments with affinity thresholds.
- Leah: benchmark scoring overhead on c6-worker and report CPU delta.
- Priya (me): draft canary run checklist and telemetry dashboard (token-util, kv-hit, p99-by-priority).

Notes-to-self / rough ideas:
- Consider using a two-tier scheduler: quick fast-path that handles the top 80% of ticks with a tiny O(1) selection, and slow-path that does full scoring when contention high.
- Might be useful to expose a per-route "batching sensitivity" flag that hints to the apportioner how tolerant a route is to reordering and batching.
